questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was crucial for me that there was opportunities to explore nature close to the exchange university.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of help to be found at uni, making it relatively easy to find information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a whole week of arranged activities for exchange students - both social and more info-oriented. The International Office at my university has been very flexible and helpful both before exchange and throughout it all.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, actually. Even though it can feel silly: Use social media and make a post that can be shared. I got help from a network, I didn't realise I had before that. And friends of friends of friends are happy to help. I found housing within days of posting.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Off-campus living can definately be less expensive as in my case, but it can also mean other logistics that you're maybe not ready to consider e.g. transportation, very specific rules from the landlord. 
I would encourage future exchange students to look for off-campus housing as well, as it can give some cultural experiences you wouldn't have had otherwise.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You had to register at the Student Help Desk in one of the main buildings of the university and then log in to your mail and the intranet. Extremely easy, quick, and straight-forward.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The student help center and the international office were both open every day. The uni website was helpful as well.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Course registration could be done online in the university's own intranet/communication platform. Here I could change and add courses on my own up until deadline for registration and cancellation. 
At HÍ there's a rule that exchange students have to have a certain amount of credits (60 %) within their own major faculty despite being on exchange on an electives semester from your home university. No exceptions.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If you want more credits than 40 for a semester e.g. if you want a language class (10 ECTS) and a weekend course (at least 2 ECTS) on top of your semester credits (30 ECTS), this cannot be done online, but has to be registered at the international office. They are very helpful, and this will only take a few minutes. 
But the advice from me would be to not overwork yourself - you will have your hands full with everything else on top of uni. Also consider the examination type and the workload/weekly hours of the course. I was very pleased with not having only oral exams or teaching every day.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had 6 ECTS on a shared BA and MA course; 10 ECTS MA course; 10 ECTS MA course (classes with the BA students); 4 ECTS in an individual research project on BA and MA level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I experienced much more group-based work at Hí than at UCPH, and a lot more professors encouraged engaging academically with your own experiences and situatedness - something I do not experience at home.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
HSP722M: Ethics of nature
HSP725M: Project in Ethics of Nature
LAN116F: Introduction to Cartography and Geovisualisation
NLF108F: Nordic Modernism and Avant-Garde - From Edith Södergran to Anarchy on the Internet

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would highly recommend Introduction to Cartography and Geovisualisation (or Cartography and map design for the BA students), if you're into this. I have a background in humanities but it was no problem for me to participate in this class; there will be something for both the cultural history, design/aesthetics oriented and software skilled students. 
Ethics of Nature is also highly recommended. Despite a bit loose structured teaching this class is an opportunity to meet people from other cultures and discuss current topics, as a lot of both Icelandic and foreign students take this class. Incredibly interesting and important syllabus.

questions.answer:
100 DKK for library card at The Nordic House.
Registration fee for the University Choir.
Fees at the doctor and the dentist (payed by my insurance).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Going out and buying food in Reykajvík is just expensive - especially if you value organic groceries as I do. 
Buying a 10-trip card to your local pool (approxiamtely 300-400 DKK) gives you a cheaper and nice way to hangout with your friends that costs you less than visits to the café.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Gym, choir, hiking trips, karaoke nights, sight-seeing bus trips.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I was happy with the university choir - also as a good base for your social life at HÍ.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Rent a car and go on a trip - get out to see the nature. Or, in the warmer seasons before the light is gone, go hitchhiking to cities or nature close by Reykavík. The hike of Esja is nice and easy to get to; Geysir and Snæfellsnes are close by as well. 
But the best tip would be to either come before uni start/stay longer to have some time to explore.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: This can be difficult. Easiest if you're both engaged in a social activity together or doing group work. But don't shy away from asking them, they're just not quite as up front as the exchange students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: More cars, less bikes. A lot more calm and laissez-faire than Copenhagen - both good and bad in the adjustment phase.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The outdoor and pool culture. And the laissez-faire attitude for sure grows on you.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Take your time to choose your classes - you can move them around after uni starts. 
Academically, you can consider this semester as more creative and free, so try out something new as you're only returning to UCPH with pass/not passed and not your usual grades. 
Seek out social activities and groups yourself while you're there. Often it isn't the speed-dating session first week that provides you with your new friend group but your courses, a random meeting, or the club/dance class/language workshop/choir/gym you've joined.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Bring wool to wear in the colder seasons, and apply for grants to ease your financial situation. Definitely don't bring books, as the national library and The Nordic House can provide you with all you need in both Danish and English. 
Biking is terrible, so make sure to have a helmet and the courage to bike around Reykjavík. Though, if you're up for it, it makes everything so much easier - and you don't have to use the unreliable buses.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know so many new friends, and living in such a wild environment and nature. To be surrounded by mountains everyday is a blessing.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The few sun hours is no joke. Take your vitamins, go to the pool, hang out with your friends a lot, eat real food. But all Icelanders feel this as well, so just embrace it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
